newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka budget hailed as pro-investment.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka budget hailed as pro-investment.

text.p: Sri Lanka's 1997 budget, which cut public spending and taxes and aims to boost exports, should lift the gloom that has hung over the country's investment climate, analysts said on Thursday.

"The budget, which is investment-friendly, should result in a rise in local and foreign investment, and dispel recent negative sentiment," said Ajit Gunewardene, director of blue chip conglomerate John Keells Holdings Ltd.

Colombo's share market reacted positively to the budget, with the all share index closing 2.78 points up at 620.67 on Thursday. Brokers said it was a feel-good response to Wednesday's "market-friendly" budget.

Sri Lanka's economy has been hit by a severe drought and power shortages this year, prompting the government to forecast growth would drop to four percent for all of 1996, down from 5.5 percent in 1995.

The budget, the third by the People's Alliance government of President Chandrika Kumaratunga, focuses on spurring the economy rather than on past concerns such as how to reduce the deficit and fight Tamil rebels, Gunewardene said.
"The budget immediately triggers off investment programmes. Also, the fact that it is for anyone who invests and is not limited to a particular sector is positive," he said.
Reduction in corporate and personal taxes were just what industrialists and consumers had sought, analysts said.
Taxes on corporate profits were lowered to 30 percent from 35 percent, and the threshold above which individual income taxes are levied was raised to 144,000 rupees a year from 100,000 rupees.
Businessmen also welcomed the budget's focus on small and medium-sized businesses, which form the backbone of an economy experiencing 13 percent unemployment.
Small investors should gain from the removal of a stamp duty of 0.5 percent, and from tax exemptions on dividends paid out by listed companies.
Sentiment, however, was not all upbeat. Some sectors are not expected to gain from the stimulus measures, analysts said.

"I am concered that depreciation on leased assets can be set off only against leasing income. It is discriminatory and in the short-term will affect share prices of commercial and investment banks," said Justin Meegoda, president and chief executive of investment bank Vanik Incorporation Ltd.
Deputy Finance Minister G.L. Peiris said the move was designed to encourage leasing, which is necessary for long-term capital formation.
Analysts also expressed concern that the budget deficit, envisaged at 98 billion rupees ($1.7 billion), would keep interest rates high.
"But the high cost of borrowing can be offset to an extent by the budget allowing exporters to borrow abroad," said Mano Tittawella, chief executive of Lanka Securities.

Colombo aims to control the budget deficit by cutting nearly four billion rupees of wasteful or less-productive state spending, while maintaining a high level of spending on infrastructure and welfare, Peiris told parliament.
